paths.reason: The repository dependency matrix and stable-interface inventory are architecture authority.
Changing the ADR enforcement boundary is itself an architecture decision.
Adding, removing, or moving governed modules changes the architecture map.
The governed UI implementation roots and contract locations define the design-first enforcement boundary.
UI change evidence fields bind tasks, reference lineage, approval ordering, and focused conformance evidence.
The design-first gate enforces human approval separation and immutable reference-before-code ordering.
The activation binds desktop conformance to one exact approved reference, target mode, normative source set, and controlled renderer.
The strict activation schema prevents conformance inputs and controlled visual settings from becoming optional or ambiguous.
The strict visual-baseline schema governs every current and historical renderer, dimension, entry, and approved-reference identity.
The visual baseline is approved-reference, browser, platform, viewport, theme, and font authority.
The shared desktop verifier enforces token, route, workflow, accessibility, responsive, and visual-reference conformance.
Desktop profile entry points must continue to invoke the governed conformance implementation.
The task schema governs exact experience-change lineage used by design-first enforcement.
Verification composition determines whether design-first enforcement is mandatory.
Quality scope determines whether the design-first checker and its regressions receive static validation.
CI policy governs the required foundation invocation that includes design-first enforcement.
The CI policy checker enforces full-history checkout and immutable base selection for design-first verification.
CI history and base selection are required to prove reference approval precedes implementation.
The review template exposes machine UI lineage and residuals to human and independent reviewers.
The systems design is the architecture baseline when no accepted ADR supersedes it.
Portable API, command, event, schema, and bundle contracts are protected interfaces.
Desktop-side transport and generated API seams are protected interfaces.
Application ports preserve replaceable infrastructure and deployment profiles.
Worker activity inputs, outputs, cancellation, progress, and failure classes are protected interfaces.
